title: Electron configurations
summary: Emission spectra show that electrons occupy fixed energy levels. Build electron configurations with sublevels and orbitals; at HL, link spectra and successive ionization energies to structure.

keyterms.definition: Pattern of specific wavelengths emitted when excited electrons fall to lower energy levels; a line spectrum for atoms.
A spectrum containing all wavelengths in a range with no gaps, such as white light passed through a prism.
A main level of fixed energy an electron can occupy, labelled n = 1, 2, 3…; levels converge at higher energy.
A division of a main energy level (s, p, d, f) containing 1, 3, 5 or 7 orbitals respectively.
A region around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron; holds up to two electrons of opposite spin.
Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d…).
Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.
An orbital holds a maximum of two electrons, which must have opposite spins.
The point where spectral lines merge into a continuum; it corresponds to the electron leaving the atom (ionization).
Energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
Energies to remove the 1st, 2nd, 3rd… electrons in turn; large jumps reveal a change of main energy level.
E = hf: the energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency, so higher-frequency light carries more energy.

questions.prompt: Why does a hydrogen atom give a line spectrum rather than a continuous one?
options: Electrons can only have certain fixed energies
Light is absorbed by the glass tube
questions.explanation: Electron energy is quantized, so transitions between levels release photons of specific energies and wavelengths.

questions.statement: In an emission spectrum, lines converge at higher energy (shorter wavelength).
questions.explanation: Energy levels get closer together as n increases, so lines crowd together towards the convergence limit.

questions.text: In the hydrogen spectrum, transitions ending at n = 2 produce lines in the ___ region.
questions.explanation: Transitions to n = 1 emit UV (larger energy gaps); transitions to n = 2 give the visible (Balmer) series.

questions.prompt: Which transition in a hydrogen atom emits the photon of highest energy?
questions.explanation: The gap between n = 2 and n = 1 is the largest of these, so the photon has the most energy (UV).

questions.prompt: Match each spectrum type to its description.

pairs.right: Bright lines on a dark background

questions.explanation: Atoms emit only specific wavelengths; white light contains all.

questions.statement: Electrons emit light when they move from a lower to a higher energy level.
questions.explanation: Absorbing energy promotes an electron to a higher level; light is emitted when it falls back to a lower level.

questions.prompt: Which colour of visible light has the highest energy?
questions.explanation: Violet has the shortest wavelength and highest frequency in the visible region, so highest photon energy.

questions.prompt: Order these regions of the electromagnetic spectrum by increasing energy.
questions.explanation: Energy rises as wavelength falls and frequency rises.

questions.text: The point where lines in an emission series merge is the ___ limit.
questions.explanation: Beyond the convergence limit the electron is no longer bound: it corresponds to ionization.

questions.prompt: Each element produces a unique line spectrum because…
options: each has a unique set of energy levels
each has a unique mass number
all atoms emit only red light
electrons are identical in every element
questions.explanation: Different nuclear charge and electron numbers give each element its own energy-level spacing, so spectra act as fingerprints.

questions.prompt: What is the full electron configuration of sulfur (Z = 16)?
questions.explanation: 16 electrons fill 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, then four go into 3p.

questions.text: The maximum number of electrons in a d sublevel is ___.
questions.explanation: A d sublevel has five orbitals, each holding two electrons.
In the Aufbau order 4s is lower in energy than 3d for the atoms in which they are filled (K, Ca), so 4s fills first.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct configuration of chromium (Z = 24)?
questions.explanation: Cr is an exception: a half-filled 3d⁵ with 4s¹ is more stable than 3d⁴ 4s².

questions.prompt: Match the sublevel to its number of orbitals.
questions.explanation: Each orbital holds two electrons, so s, p, d, f hold 2, 6, 10, 14.

questions.statement: Hund's rule says the three 2p electrons of nitrogen occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins.
questions.explanation: Degenerate orbitals fill singly first, minimizing repulsion.

questions.prompt: What is the configuration of Fe²⁺ (Z = 26)?
questions.explanation: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Transition metals lose 4s electrons first, giving [Ar] 3d⁶.

questions.prompt: Order these sublevels by the sequence in which they fill.
questions.explanation: Aufbau order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p…

questions.text: Two electrons in the same orbital must have opposite spins, according to the ___ exclusion principle.
questions.explanation: Pauli: at most two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins.

questions.prompt: Which shape describes a p orbital?
questions.explanation: s orbitals are spherical; each p orbital is dumbbell-shaped, along x, y or z.

questions.prompt: Why does first ionization energy generally increase across period 3?
options: Electrons are removed from d orbitals
Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same
questions.explanation: Electrons are added to the same shell, so increasing nuclear charge holds them more tightly.

questions.statement: The first ionization energy of aluminium is lower than that of magnesium.
questions.explanation: Al's outer electron is in 3p, which is higher in energy and more shielded than Mg's 3s electron.

questions.prompt: Why is the first IE of sulfur lower than that of phosphorus?
options: S loses an electron from a doubly occupied 3p orbital, where pairing repulsion helps removal
S has a smaller nuclear charge
questions.explanation: In S (3p⁴) one 3p orbital holds a pair; repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove.

questions.text: An element has successive IEs (kJ mol⁻¹) 578, 1817, 2745, 11 577. It is in group ___.
questions.explanation: The big jump comes after the third electron, so there are three outer electrons: group 13 (aluminium).

questions.statement: Successive ionization energies of an element always increase.
questions.explanation: Each electron is removed from an increasingly positive ion, so more energy is needed each time.

questions.prompt: The convergence limit of the hydrogen Lyman series (transitions to n = 1) corresponds to…
options: the energy of a red photon
questions.explanation: At convergence the electron is excited from n = 1 to n = ∞, which is ionization.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its relationship.
questions.explanation: E = hf and c = fλ combine to E = hc/λ.

questions.prompt: Order these period-2 elements by first ionization energy, lowest first.
questions.explanation: General increase across the period, with dips at B (2p electron) and O; so Li < B < Be < C < N.

questions.prompt: Which equation represents the first ionization energy of sodium?
questions.explanation: IE is defined for gaseous atoms forming gaseous ions.

questions.text: A photon has frequency 6.0 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹. With h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, its energy is ___ × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
